chunks: What is galvanic isolation?. The question: What is galvanic isolation?
Galvanic isolation means two circuits have no direct conductive path between them, so no steady current can flow from one to the other.
They can still exchange information or power, using light, a magnetic field or an electric field across a thin gap.
It lets the two sides sit at very different voltages and keeps a fault on one side from reaching the other.
It is not perfect: fast voltage jumps can still leak across the small capacitance (charge-storing ability) of the barrier.
Picture two rooms separated by a thick glass wall. You can wave, and the person inside sees you. You can tap on the glass and they feel the vibration. But nobody can walk through.
A very hard slam, though, can rattle things on the other side. That slam is a fast voltage edge passing through the barrier capacitance.
The analogy leaves out power: the far room still needs its own heater, meaning its own supply.
Information (and energy) crosses through a transmitter, a non-conductive coupling medium and a receiver. The two grounds are separate and can sit at different potentials.
Conductive path: a route where steady (DC) current can flow, such as a wire or a shared ground.
Barrier capacitance ( C iso ): the small capacitance across the gap, around 1 picofarads in a signal isolator.
Common-mode voltage: a voltage that appears on both wires of one side relative to the other side's reference.
CMTI: the fastest common-mode voltage edge the isolator tolerates without error.
Working voltage: the voltage the barrier can withstand continuously, which is lower than the short test voltage.
Take a 1 picofarads barrier.
A capacitor passes no steady current at all, and at 1 megahertz it still acts like a 1 over (2 pi times 10 to the 6 times 10 to the -12) equals 159 kilohms resistor.
But a fast edge of 50 volts/ns pushes 1 picofarads times 50 volts over ns equals 50 milliamps across, which can cause glitches.
So isolation blocks steady and slow stuff well and fast edges poorly. That is the whole idea.

"Galvanic isolation means two circuits have no direct conductive path, so no DC current, yet they still exchange signal or power through light, a magnetic field or an electric field across a capacitor.
It lets the two sides sit at completely different voltages, breaks ground loops and contains faults.
But the barrier has a little capacitance, so fast common-mode transients still cross, it has a finite voltage rating, and the far side still needs its own isolated supply."
